interactions.label: Why is growth faltering considered one of the most valuable early warning signs

params.question: Why is growth faltering considered one of the most valuable early warning signs in paediatric practice?

answers.text: It is easily detected by parents without medical training

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Growth faltering requires serial anthropometric measurements plotted on a growth chart to detect. Parents may notice a child looks thin, but quantifying the deviation from the expected trajectory requires clinical measurement.

answers.text: It can appear weeks to months before any clinical signs of illness or malnutrition

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Growth faltering — a sustained drop in a child's weight-for-age percentile — often precedes overt clinical signs, making it a uniquely sensitive early indicator of underlying illness or nutritional inadequacy.

answers.text: It is diagnostic of a specific nutritional deficiency

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Growth faltering is a nonspecific signal. It may indicate malnutrition, chronic infection, hormonal deficiency, or psychosocial deprivation — further evaluation is needed to identify the specific cause.

answers.text: It occurs only in children below the age of six months

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Growth faltering can occur at any age during childhood. It is especially significant in infancy because growth velocity is at its highest and most fragile during this period, but it is by no means limited to the first six months.

overallFeedback.feedback: Growth faltering is important because it appears weeks to months before clinical signs of illness or malnutrition become apparent, making it one of the earliest detectable warning signs in paediatric practice.
Growth faltering is clinically powerful because it appears before overt signs of disease or malnutrition, giving clinicians a crucial window for early intervention.

interactions.label: Which of the following is the single strongest predictor of a child's final adul

params.question: Which of the following is the single strongest predictor of a child's final adult height?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Birth weight reflects intrauterine growth but is not the strongest predictor of final adult height. A child born small for gestational age may show catch-up growth and reach normal adult height if other factors are favourable.

answers.text: Nutritional intake in the first year of life

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Nutrition is a critical extrinsic factor that supports growth, but when adequate nutrition is available, the genetic component — primarily familial stature — is the stronger determinant of final height.

Correct. Familial stature is the strongest predictor of final adult height. Tall parents tend to have tall children, and short parents tend to have shorter children, provided the environment supports normal growth.

Growth hormone is the main postnatal driver of linear growth, but its effect operates within the limits set by a child's genetic potential. Familial stature, reflecting the cumulative genetic contribution, is the stronger overall predictor.

overallFeedback.feedback: Familial stature is the single strongest predictor of a child's final adult height. Genetic influences from both parents shape target height, body proportions, and even the tempo of growth.
Genetics sets the ceiling for growth. When the environment is supportive, parental stature is the most reliable predictor of how tall a child will eventually become.

interactions.label: A health worker is about to measure a 30-month-old child's length using an infan

params.question: A health worker is about to measure a 30-month-old child's length using an infantometer in the supine position. What should be corrected about this approach?

answers.text: The child should be weighed instead of measured for length

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both weight and length (or height) are essential anthropometric parameters. The issue here is the technique being used for this age group, not the parameter being measured.

answers.text: The child should be measured standing using a stadiometer

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. After two years of age, children must be measured standing using a stadiometer. Recumbent length on an infantometer is used only for children under two. This matters because recumbent length is typically 0.5–0.7 cm greater than standing height due to spinal compression.

answers.text: The child's head circumference should be measured first

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Head circumference is important but unrelated to the error here. The fundamental problem is using a supine length measurement for a child who has passed the two-year transition point to standing height.

answers.text: The measurement should be repeated three times and averaged

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While repeated measurements improve precision, the key error here is using the wrong method for the child's age. Recumbent length should switch to standing height at two years — no amount of repetition corrects a systematic technique error.

overallFeedback.feedback: After two years of age, children must be measured standing (height) using a stadiometer, not supine (length) on an infantometer. This WHO-standardised transition ensures measurement consistency across serial assessments.
At two years of age, anthropometric technique switches from supine length to standing height. Using the wrong method introduces systematic error and compromises growth chart interpretation.

interactions.label: Developmental screening is the ongoing process of observing whether a child meet

params.question: Developmental screening is the ongoing process of observing whether a child meets age-appropriate milestones at every clinical visit.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This describes developmental monitoring, not screening. Monitoring is the ongoing observation at every clinical visit. Screening is a separate step — a brief standardised test given to all children at specific ages. The cascade runs: monitoring → screening → evaluation, and each step serves a distinct purpose.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this describes developmental monitoring, not screening. Monitoring is the ongoing observation at every clinical contact. Screening is a different step: a brief standardised test given to all children at specific ages. Together with evaluation, they form a three-level cascade: monitoring detects a concern, screening confirms it, and evaluation diagnoses it.

interactions.label: A 12-month-old infant born at 28 weeks of gestation cannot yet sit without suppo

params.question: A 12-month-old infant born at 28 weeks of gestation cannot yet sit without support. The parents are worried about motor delay. What is the essential first step before concluding that a developmental delay exists?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Neuroimaging may eventually be warranted if a true delay is confirmed, but the first step is to determine whether a delay actually exists. For a premature infant, this requires assessing milestones using corrected age, not chronological age.

answers.text: Reassure the parents that premature infants always catch up by age two

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Blanket reassurance is inappropriate — not all premature infants catch up spontaneously. The clinician must first adjust for prematurity by using corrected age. A 12-month-old born at 28 weeks has a corrected age of only about 9 months.

answers.text: Assess the child's milestones using corrected age rather than chronological age

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A child born at 28 weeks is approximately 12 weeks (3 months) premature. At a chronological age of 12 months, the corrected age is about 9 months. Independent sitting is expected by 8–9 months — so this child may actually be on track when corrected age is applied.

answers.text: Start physiotherapy immediately without waiting for a formal diagnosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Beginning therapy before establishing whether a true delay exists is premature. The essential first step for a preterm infant is to use corrected age for milestone assessment — this may reveal that the child is actually developing normally for their adjusted age.

overallFeedback.feedback: Prematurity requires correction of age when assessing developmental milestones. A 12-month-old born at 28 weeks has a corrected age of approximately 9 months, which changes milestone expectations significantly.
For any premature infant, corrected age must be used when assessing developmental milestones. This adjustment prevents overdiagnosis of delay and ensures appropriate clinical decisions.
